```kotlin
    test("rational timestamp reports overflow") {
        expectFailure<ArithmeticException> { presentationUs(Long.MAX_VALUE, 24, 1001) }
    }
    test("RAW-derived label requires RAW origin") { validateLabel(Origin.RAW, "raw-derived") }
    test("SDR cannot be promoted by an output label") {
        expectFailure<IllegalArgumentException> { validateLabel(Origin.SDR, "raw-derived") }
    }
    test("HLG remains HDR-derived") { validateLabel(Origin.HLG, "hdr-derived") }
    test("HLG does not become proprietary Samsung Log") {
        expectFailure<IllegalArgumentException> { validateLabel(Origin.HLG, "native-samsung-log") }
    }
    test("graph rejects incompatible transfer contracts") {
        val a = Signal("AWG3", "LINEAR", 16); val b = Signal("AWG3", "LOGC3", 16)
        expectFailure<IllegalArgumentException> { requireCompatible(a, b) }
    }
    test("graph rejects a hidden precision change") {
        expectFailure<IllegalArgumentException> {
            requireCompatible(Signal("AWG3", "LINEAR", 16), Signal("AWG3", "LINEAR", 8))
        }
    }
    test("graph accepts identical declared signals") {
        val a = Signal("AWG3", "LINEAR", 16); requireCompatible(a, a)
    }
    test("manual readiness requires current matching generation") {
        check(!manualReady(ManualTarget(5, 10000000, 100), ManualResult(4, 10000000, 100, true)))
    }
    test("AE-off alone does not establish exposure match") {
        check(!manualReady(ManualTarget(5, 10000000, 100), ManualResult(5, 20000000, 100, true)))
    }
    test("missing manual metadata stays unready") {
        check(!manualReady(ManualTarget(5, 10000000, 100), ManualResult(5, null, 100, true)))
    }
    test("matching manual result establishes model readiness") {
        check(manualReady(ManualTarget(5, 10000000, 100), ManualResult(5, 10000000, 100, true)))
    }
    test("active auto exposure blocks manual readiness") {
        check(!manualReady(ManualTarget(5, 10000000, 100), ManualResult(5, 10000000, 100, false)))
    }
    test("focus plane has zero geometric blur") { check(abs(cocMm(50.0, 2.0, 2000.0, 2000.0)) < 1e-12) }
    test("infinity has finite signed geometric blur") {
        check(abs(cocMm(50.0, 2.0, 2000.0, Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY) - 0.6410256410256411) < 1e-12)
    }
    test("foreground and background blur retain opposite signs") {
        check(cocMm(50.0, 2.0, 2000.0, 1000.0) < 0)
        check(cocMm(50.0, 2.0, 2000.0, 4000.0) > 0)
    }
    test("optics rejects NaN and impossible focus geometry") {
        expectFailure<IllegalArgumentException> { cocMm(50.0, Double.NaN, 2000.0, 1000.0) }
        expectFailure<IllegalArgumentException> { cocMm(50.0, 2.0, 40.0, 1000.0) }
    }
    println("RESULT passed=$passed failed=$failed")
    check(failed == 0) { "$failed contract tests failed" }
}
```


<a id="android-adaptation"></a>
## Appendix B. Android implementation handbook, test adapters, and experimental protocols

### B.1 Status of the examples in this appendix

The Python and Kotlin files in Appendix A are the executed reference code. The Android, shader, SQL, JSON, and shell examples in this appendix are implementation patterns and proposed contracts. They were not compiled against the Android repository during preparation of this document. They must be adapted to the inspected production interfaces and put through the same red–green process before integration. Do not paste an example into a release and infer that its presence in this directive establishes compatibility.

The examples deliberately avoid prescribing a replacement UI framework, a second camera engine, or a new dependency tree. Their purpose is to identify boundaries that must be made testable. Existing correct implementations should be reused. An agent should first locate the corresponding production behavior, then add a characterization test, then make the smallest change needed to satisfy the contract.

When an example names a conceptual type that does not exist in the repository, treat that name as an interface role rather than an instruction to duplicate functionality. The final production name should follow the repository's conventions. Any proposed file path in a test plan is a logical location, not permission to create a parallel application.

### B.2 Camera image ownership: test the adapter, not merely the helper

Android image buffers have a lifecycle separate from the UI and from any copied byte array. The test adapter must therefore distinguish an owned image, a borrowed plane view, an application-owned copy, and a released resource. A buffer view remaining reachable in Kotlin does not prove that the underlying camera resource is still valid. Media and image API ownership should be reviewed against the relevant Android contracts.[^A04][^A05]

The following pattern illustrates an adapter around the portable lease. It does not make image access magically thread-safe. Its caller still owns the responsibility to finish reading before closing or transferring the lease. Never call `get()` on one thread while another thread may close the same image. A production implementation can instead provide a scoped callback or explicit queue transfer when that better enforces ownership.

```kotlin
// Android integration pattern; compile and instrument inside the actual project.
import android.media.Image
import cinema.reference.FrameLease

fun ownCameraImage(image: Image): FrameLease<Image> =
    FrameLease(image) { image.close() }

fun <T> readAndRelease(image: Image, copy: (Image) -> T): T {
    val lease = ownCameraImage(image)
    return try {
        copy(lease.get())
    } finally {
        lease.close()
    }
}
```

Write the first adapter test with a fake close-counting resource and a copy operation that throws halfway through. The expected outcome is exactly one release and no queued partially initialized frame. Add a second test where queue admission fails: the rejected image must be released immediately. Add a third where ownership successfully transfers: the producer must not close the image before the consumer completes. Then repeat the essential lifecycle tests with actual Android image callbacks on an available device or suitable instrumentation environment.

A queue capacity expressed only as an image count is incomplete when modes have different dimensions. Maintain both count and byte budgets. The byte estimate must include copied payload, metadata, alignment, and any temporary conversion buffers. Record the admission decision in diagnostics. A rejected archival frame is an acquisition integrity event, not a harmless preview drop.

### B.3 Separate control intent, effective request, and observed result

Manual camera controls require at least three representations. The user's draft expresses intent. The effective request expresses what the application submitted after applying the selected mode's bounds. The observed result expresses what the camera reported for a particular frame. Do not collapse these into one slider value.

The readiness gate should consume a recent result from the current session generation. It must check the relevant fields, their tolerances, and any required convergence or lock state. An old matching result is not enough after a new request or route change. A reported automatic-exposure-off state is not proof that the requested exposure time and sensitivity were applied. The portable Kotlin example demonstrates part of this distinction but omits production freshness and request-sequence policy.

A useful test table includes a matching result, a stale generation, missing exposure, missing sensitivity, active automatic exposure, an effective request clamped by the mode, and a result outside tolerance. For each row, assert the readiness state and the exact user-facing explanation category. Do not assert a long localized message in the domain test; assert a stable reason code and test localization separately.

```json
{
  "control_contract_version": 1,
  "generation": 12,
  "intent": {"exposure_ns": 20000000, "iso": 100},
  "effective_request": {"exposure_ns": 16666666, "iso": 100},
  "observed_result": null,
  "readiness": "pending_result",
  "reason": "awaiting_current_generation_metadata"
}
```

The example values illustrate a distinction, not a measured S23 mode. A test must not conclude that a particular exposure is available merely because the schema accepts the number. During recording, control changes need an explicit policy: allowed and recorded as time-varying metadata, deferred until the next take, or rejected. The application must not change policies silently when the screen rotates.

### B.4 RAW source validation precedes image development

Treat every retained or imported RAW source as potentially truncated, malformed, or mismatched. Validate the header before allocating image-sized buffers. Check version, dimensions, format, CFA, declared record size, metadata length, timestamp ordering, and source identity. Bound arithmetic used to compute row and frame sizes so integer overflow cannot turn a huge input into a small accepted allocation.

For a row-strided source, calculate required bytes from the actual layout rather than assuming tightly packed pixels. A raw format label is not enough to infer byte order or bit placement. Keep format-specific unpackers small, separately tested, and explicit about supported variants. Unknown layouts should fail with a useful reason and preserve the source for later analysis.

Test corruption at every boundary: before the first complete frame, in a metadata record, inside a pixel row, immediately after a complete frame, and inside the final record. The ordinary developer should not silently reinterpret a truncated file as complete. A separate recovery tool may expose a verified prefix, but it must label that output as recovered and retain the original.

After validation, development should remain streaming where practical. A source reader supplies bounded rows or tiles and their metadata; the developer consumes them through a well-defined interface. Avoid making every correction stage load a full-resolution float image. The reference implementation should prioritize correctness, while an accelerated implementation is checked against it using the same source and profile identities.

### B.5 P010 tests must inspect bytes, strides, and color interpretation

P010 is not merely a request for a ten-bit codec profile. A buffer-input path needs an actual supported image layout, correct placement of ten-bit samples in sixteen-bit storage, correct handling of row and pixel strides, correct luma/chroma geometry, and a compatible encoder. The Android format and codec contracts are the starting point; observed plane metadata determines the actual access pattern.[^A04][^A05]

The portable Python functions deliberately operate on a single row so the bit-placement rule can be tested independently. Extend them with fixtures for padded rows, nonzero crop origins, two-plane and three-plane representations only where documented and supported, and extreme legal sample values. Fill padding with a sentinel and verify that the implementation does not read it as image data or overwrite memory outside the owned range.

The color transform producing Y, Cb, and Cr must declare its coefficients and range separately from the RGB primaries and transfer function. A BT.709 matrix used for YUV storage does not imply that the RGB image has Rec.709 primaries. When a delivery format cannot fully signal the intended Log/gamut combination, preserve an explicit sidecar and test the documented consumer assignment. Do not replace unknown transfer metadata with HLG simply because that makes a phone preview look plausible.

A precision test should include known ten-bit ramps, a deliberately eight-bit-degraded control, color patches, and spatial detail. Decode independently and compare the intended sample domain. Container metadata, successful playback, or a large number of interpolated output values is insufficient by itself. Keep codec-path precision evidence separate from evidence about the original camera source.

### B.6 Keep exposure encoding and display rendering in separate nodes

The LogC3 reference is an encoding of a declared scene-oriented signal. It is not the film look, a white-balance operation, or a display tone map. A graph node implementing it must accept the correct working primaries and exposure convention, preserve the signed branch where specified, and report any output-domain clipping at the delivery boundary.

The following GLSL helper illustrates the same published EI800 exposure-domain function as the Python reference. It is a function-level pattern, not a complete shader pipeline. The actual GPU implementation must be compiled for its supported backend, compared against the CPU reference, and tested for precision and range handling. It must not be inserted after a display transform while retaining a scene-linear input label.[^C01]

```glsl
// Function-level reference pattern; GPU compilation and differential tests are required.
highp float logc3_ei800(highp float x) {
    const highp float cut = 0.010591;
    const highp float a = 5.555556;
    const highp float b = 0.052272;
    const highp float c = 0.247190;
    const highp float d = 0.385537;
    const highp float e = 5.367655;
    const highp float f = 0.092809;
    if (x > cut) {
        return c * log(a * x + b) / log(10.0) + d;
    }
    return e * x + f;
}
```

The differential fixture should include negative values, black, middle grey, the join point on both sides, values above scene-linear one, and large finite values inside the declared implementation domain. Compare both absolute and relative error where appropriate. A test limited to values from zero to one misses important Log behavior. A test that clamps its input before comparison can hide the defect it is supposed to detect.

The preview branch applies a viewing transform exactly once. A clean Log master must not receive that viewing transform accidentally through a shared render target. Test monitor independence by toggling overlays, display brightness controls, and viewing transforms while comparing clean output pixels or hashes under deterministic synthetic input.

### B.7 GPU precision is a graph property

Do not select one precision globally and assume it is adequate for every stage. A matrix transform, a long blur accumulation, a logarithm, a density response, and an alpha-compositing operation have different error behavior. Use a high-precision CPU reference to locate sensitive stages, then choose the least expensive tested representation that stays within the declared budget.

A backend capability record should distinguish texture sampling, rendering, storage-image access, filtering, import, export, and synchronization support. The presence of a graphics API version is not proof that every required format and usage combination works. Query the actual features and attempt a controlled operation before enabling a route. The Khronos specification defines API behavior, not the S23's complete tested capability set.[^G01]

Test repeated accumulation using bright impulses on dark backgrounds. Such fixtures reveal overflow, cancellation, and banding that ordinary footage may conceal. Test values outside the display range without clipping them prematurely. Test every required alpha convention. Compare an untiled reference with multiple tile sizes, including boundaries through bright point sources and high-contrast edges.

Resource synchronization needs its own tests. Delay completion deliberately, reuse pools aggressively, cancel a job mid-flight, and recreate the rendering context. An accepted frame must never contain data from a newer or older frame because a buffer was recycled too early. Record fences or equivalent completion evidence in development diagnostics without placing unbounded logging on the capture-critical path.

### B.8 Stock response: fit constraints before aesthetic tuning

Begin with a stock-model interface that separates incident exposure, channel response, density, development parameters, print interpretation, and final display rendering. A stock profile is not just three arbitrary curves with a famous name attached. It needs provenance, a stated reconstruction level, and a validation domain.

For a first reference model, use a smooth monotonic response with explicit toe, middle region, and shoulder. Constrain fits so local interpolation cannot reverse exposure ordering. Test the curve over a dense domain, not only at control points. Preserve the distinction between a mathematical toy used to test the engine and a fitted interpretation based on appropriate references.

A useful fitting objective can combine weighted residuals to measured density or color observations, smoothness regularization, neutral constraints, and penalties for invalid response. The weights and regularization are project choices and must be recorded. Fit on one subset and evaluate on held-out exposures and colors. Do not tune the model while looking at every validation frame and then call the result independent validation.

The renderer should expose exposure before the negative response separately from printing or final grading. The same numerical slider position applied at different graph locations can produce different highlight, shadow, and grain behavior. Tests should deliberately move the operation to the wrong location and confirm that the graph contract or image oracle detects it.

Stock names must remain honest. A provisional “500T interpretation” may be useful, but it must not become a measured reproduction merely because its colors are appealing. Kodak's technical material constrains the research; it does not supply every parameter of a finished digital emulation.[^F03]

### B.9 Grain: coordinates, density, sampling, and compression

The grain subsystem needs two layers of tests. The first layer tests deterministic execution: the same seed, frame identity, spatial coordinates, channel, graph version, and profile must produce the same reference sample. Tiling, chunking, cancellation, and resumption must not shift the random field. The second layer tests the intended image statistics and appearance under exposure and output-size changes.

A counter-based random function is useful because it avoids storing a mutable random stream for every tile. It is not, by itself, a physical film-grain model. The reference Gaussian sampler exists to test coordinate identity and reproducibility. A production model should investigate material structure, channel relationships, exposure-dependent behavior, and the relationship between virtual film area and output sampling. Published grain-rendering research provides a relevant methodological reference.[^F01]

Test grain before and after resizing with an explicit comparison procedure. A simple texture pasted at fixed screen-pixel size will change its implied physical scale when output dimensions change. Conversely, aggressively resampling fine grain can erase it or create aliasing. The renderer must state where grain is synthesized and how it is integrated over output pixels.

Compression changes grain appearance and bitrate demand. Evaluate the final delivery file, not only an uncompressed preview. Compare dark textured scenes, smooth skies, skin, and saturated lights. A codec that smears temporal grain can alter the intended look even when average color error is small. Do not compensate by adding excessive grain without investigating the delivery settings.

### B.10 Halation and bloom: energy and ordering tests

Treat halation and optical bloom as separate model components with explicit domains and parameters. A bright-region glow applied indiscriminately in display space may create a recognizable effect, but it does not automatically reproduce either physical process. The production renderer should document whether a component is physically motivated, empirically fitted, or deliberately stylized.

Construct an impulse fixture with a controlled bright source against a dark field. Measure the radial or directional response, channel behavior, energy normalization, and spatial support. Repeat at different incident exposures and virtual-format scales. Position the impulse on tile boundaries to expose insufficient halos. Test a neutral bright object and a saturated bright object separately.

Thresholds should be defined in the model's declared exposure or density domain. A threshold tied only to the final eight-bit display value can behave differently after a viewing transform changes. If a creative threshold is used, name it as such and keep it distinct from a physical parameter.

Do not let halation become a universal red outline detector. Fine dark/light edges, skin highlights, specular metal, and clipped sources should receive separate scrutiny. Record where source clipping prevents meaningful reconstruction. A plausible highlight roll-off cannot restore detail that was never captured, and the interface should not imply otherwise.

### B.11 Virtual format and lens parameter contracts

The virtual format defines an image-area geometry and sampling relationship. It does not automatically choose a color grade. A lens interpretation defines focal geometry, aperture behavior, distortion, vignetting, aberrations, focus breathing, and point-spread assumptions as supported by the implementation. Keep these components independently versioned.

The ideal thin-lens model is a useful reference for defocus sign and magnitude, not a complete description of a real cinema lens. Its geometric f-number must not be replaced by a T-stop without a declared relationship. A T-stop describes transmission-related exposure behavior; a geometric aperture model needs the pupil geometry. The interface can show a transmission control and an optical aperture control separately when exact lens data is unavailable.

Test field-of-view consistency when changing virtual gate size and focal length. A matched field of view should not silently change the captured viewpoint. Cropping changes available image area and output resolution; it does not move the camera. A requested lens view wider than the source cannot be recovered through a label change.

For relative-depth operation, expose a creative focus target and bounded defocus parameter rather than invented distance readouts. For metric-depth operation, require a calibration contract and uncertainty. A focus distance of two metres should mean two metres only when that statement has been validated for the selected depth pipeline.

### B.12 Depth inference: normalization and output semantics

Model integration begins with an exact input/output specification. Record color ordering, transfer state, resize policy, aspect handling, normalization constants, tensor layout, supported dimensions, output scale convention, invalid-value behavior, and expected precision. A model that appears to produce plausible depth can still be wrong because RGB and BGR were swapped or the input was gamma-encoded differently from training.

Build a preprocessing test using small synthetic color blocks whose expected tensor values are easy to calculate independently. Verify each channel and spatial position. Build an output-decoding test with a known tensor and assert its orientation, crop, units, and invalid mask. Do not test only the final visualization because a normalized heat map can hide scale and layout errors.

The model registry must bind behavior to an exact weight hash and conversion identity. Quantized and unquantized versions are different artifacts. Delegate-specific conversions require their own comparison tests. If a model update changes relative-depth scale or temporal behavior, old jobs must retain the old model or explicitly migrate to a new render identity.

Qualcomm's deployment entry makes on-device experimentation plausible, while the upstream model projects provide implementation and licensing details. Neither establishes that the complete proposed pipeline sustains a particular recording frame rate on the user's phone. Measure initialization, inference, transfers, rendering, encoding, and thermal behavior together.[^D02][^D03][^D04]

### B.13 Temporal depth alignment before smoothing

Temporal consistency is not achieved by averaging consecutive depth maps at the same pixel coordinates. Camera and object motion change correspondences. Relative-depth scale may also change. A temporal module must therefore establish valid correspondence, align the declared depth representation where justified, reject invalid history, and then blend according to confidence.

A proposed reference sequence is: compute or obtain flow; evaluate forward/backward consistency; exclude occlusions and uncertain boundaries; estimate a robust alignment between current and reprojected historical relative depth; reject an unsupported fit; combine aligned values with confidence-dependent weights; and reset state at scene discontinuities. Each operation needs its own fixture and failure policy.

For affine alignment of a relative inverse-depth representation, state the exact model and fitting domain. Do not fit arbitrary scale and offset using every pixel indiscriminately. Foreground motion, reflections, invalid regions, and scene cuts can dominate the fit. Use held-out correspondences to check whether the alignment generalizes within the frame.

Test a stationary background with a new near object entering the frame. Independent min-max normalization will often alter all normalized background values; the test should detect the resulting focus pumping. Then test camera translation, rotation, disocclusion, and hard cuts. The accepted behavior may reduce temporal reuse rather than force a confident but wrong estimate.

### B.14 Matting and mixed pixels

Hair, transparent material, motion blur, and glass do not fit a simple opaque binary-mask model. Their pixels can contain mixtures of foreground and background radiance. A depth map usually does not fully describe those mixtures. Treat matting and boundary refinement as separate estimates with their own uncertainty, not as a cosmetic dilation of the subject mask.

A reference compositing test should use known foreground color, background color, and alpha. Verify premultiplied versus straight-alpha conventions and the effect of blur ordering. A renderer that blurs colors without respecting coverage can create bright or dark fringes. The test should include both bright foreground against dark background and the reverse arrangement.

Do not assume that a perfect alpha mask solves every missing-background problem. Defocusing a foreground object can reveal contributions that were not visible in the source. The renderer must use a declared approximation, reduce the effect where uncertainty is high, or allow manual intervention. Generative replacement of unseen content is not a default requirement of this project.

Evaluate boundary stability over complete clips. Save diagnostic mattes and confidence maps during development, but judge the final effect at normal playback speed as well. A boundary that looks acceptable in one frame may shimmer across time. The release policy should limit aggressive blur settings when the estimator cannot support them reliably.

### B.15 Layered bokeh and occlusion-aware rendering

A physically motivated blur footprint varies with depth and lens parameters. The renderer must preserve foreground/background ordering and normalize contributions appropriately. Uniformly blurring everything outside a person mask cannot reproduce this behavior, especially when foreground objects are also defocused.

Begin with perfect synthetic depth and simple opaque layers. This separates renderer defects from estimator defects. Test a sharp foreground occluder, a defocused foreground object, an in-focus subject, and bright background points. Inspect whether light leaks through opaque surfaces, whether energy changes unexpectedly, and whether foreground coverage expands plausibly under defocus.

Then add estimated depth and compare the difference. This ablation identifies how much error comes from depth, matting, or rendering. Keep the perfect-depth reference available even after the production pipeline becomes complex. It is a valuable oracle for regressions that would otherwise be blamed on the model.

Aperture shape, cat-eye behavior, longitudinal chromatic effects, and anamorphic characteristics should be introduced only after the basic layered renderer is stable. Each feature adds parameters and potential temporal artifacts. Provide a neutral reference mode with those embellishments disabled so the core geometry remains testable.

### B.16 Focus interaction and focus transitions

Tap-to-focus must resolve a target in the rendered scene rather than merely store a screen coordinate forever. The application should define how the target is tracked, what happens during occlusion, and how it behaves when the target leaves the frame. An automatic nearest-face rule must not silently replace a user-selected subject.

A focus transition needs a temporal curve, duration policy, depth representation, and target-loss policy. It should not jump because a single noisy depth estimate changes. Conversely, excessive smoothing must not create a long lag that makes the control unusable. Test both numerical continuity and perceived responsiveness.

Use a sequence with two subjects crossing. Select one explicitly and verify identity retention under the declared tracking policy. Then remove that subject from view and inspect the displayed state. A defensible behavior is to hold, relax, or ask for a new target according to a documented setting; pretending the target remains confidently tracked is not acceptable.

Accessibility matters here. Provide alternatives to precise tapping, readable focus-state text, and controls that remain usable with larger text and screen readers. Do not make the only way to correct a focus error a tiny draggable point on a moving preview. Test the interaction independently of the final optical quality.


### B.17 Motion rendering and shutter interpretation

Motion blur belongs to exposure over time, not simply to a spatial blur filter. The captured source already contains motion integrated over its actual exposure interval. A synthetic shutter operation must therefore declare whether it adds an approximation, interpolates intermediate images, or combines genuinely captured frames. It must not imply that a long blurred exposure can always be converted into a short sharp one.

For a simple reference, the exposure duration associated with a shutter angle is the angle divided by 360, multiplied by the frame period. The included Python function tests that arithmetic using a rational rate. This establishes a timing relationship, not a complete motion renderer. A production effect needs correspondence, occlusion handling, boundary behavior, and a policy for source blur already present.

Construct a synthetic sequence with a bright moving object crossing a dark field at known speed. Compare the expected integrated path with the renderer's result. Then add an occluder and verify that hidden motion does not leak through it. Test a scene cut so frames from unrelated shots are not averaged together. Include an object entering or leaving the frame, where temporal support is incomplete.

Record whether the operation changes frame count, presentation timestamps, or apparent speed. The original timing must remain in the source manifest. If interpolation is enabled, label the derivative accordingly and retain the clean master. Do not use interpolated frames to claim a source recording rate the camera did not achieve.

### B.18 Stabilization, rolling shutter, and crop accounting

Stabilization can improve usability, but it changes the relationship between the source image, output crop, and virtual lens. The renderer must track the transformation applied to each frame so depth, flow, masks, and focus coordinates remain aligned. Applying a crop to the color image but not to its depth map is a serious geometry defect even when the preview looks approximately correct.

Begin with a known synthetic camera motion and a static scene. Verify transform direction, coordinate convention, interpolation, and crop boundaries. Then introduce independent object motion and ensure the estimator does not treat the entire scene as one rigid plane. A global transform is a deliberate model choice, not an exact explanation of all motion.

Rolling-shutter correction requires additional assumptions about readout and motion. Do not enable a physically labeled correction using an invented readout time. Treat unmeasured correction as an experimental approximation and record its parameter source. Test vertical and horizontal structures, fast pans, and independently moving objects. A correction that straightens one feature while distorting another must be evaluated on the whole clip.

Display the retained field of view and any output-resolution reduction honestly. A stabilized image cropped from a larger source is not equivalent to native capture at the same final framing. Preserve the original transform history so a later development can choose a different stabilization setting without recapturing the scene.

### B.19 Denoising must preserve evidence and intended texture

Phone noise and simulated film grain are different phenomena. Denoising the source and adding controlled film texture can be useful, but the process must not erase detail and then conceal that loss behind grain. Keep denoising optional, versioned, and separate from the stock model.

A reference denoising fixture should include fine static texture, moving texture, skin-like smooth regions, dark gradients, and bright edges. Temporal methods need tests for ghosting and delayed trails. Spatial methods need tests for detail loss and edge halos. Evaluate differences before film grain is added so the texture effect cannot mask a defect.

For RAW-derived processing, noise behavior may vary with exposure, sensitivity, channel, and readout mode. A noise model must identify its measured domain. Do not reuse one attractive noise estimate across every camera route or firmware without validation. For processed SDR/HLG sources, acknowledge that upstream denoising and sharpening may already be irreversible.

The clean-master policy needs a precise meaning here. Retain the original acquisition separately from a developed master that includes optional denoising. A user should be able to return to the less-processed source. If storage constraints lead to an explicit deletion choice, show which file is irreplaceable and which can be regenerated from retained inputs.

### B.20 Color protection should remain an explicit creative tool

Skin, skies, and other familiar regions can be useful subjects for color evaluation, but the renderer should not secretly apply scene-dependent corrections that make a stock model impossible to reproduce. If semantic masks influence color, those masks and parameters become part of the saved graph and model identity.

A simple first implementation should favor globally coherent color transforms with well-characterized behavior. Add selective protection only when a measured failure justifies it. For example, a user may choose a bounded skin-hue protection control as a creative feature, but the app must not claim that this reproduces a particular film stock's physical response.

Test a scene containing multiple people, varied complexions, colored lighting, and objects with similar hues. A semantic correction should not assume that every orange or brown region is skin. It must preserve the user's intended lighting rather than neutralize colored illumination automatically. No sensitive identity inference is needed for this project.

Compare the effect on and off using identical input and a saved mask visualization. Check temporal stability so the color does not pulse as a detector changes confidence. Provide a graceful fallback when the model cannot identify a region reliably. The user should retain control over whether the selective effect is applied.

### B.21 A persistent job state machine

A development queue should persist explicit states rather than infer completion from a filename. The following SQL is a schema pattern, not a migration ready to run against the existing application. Adapt it to the repository's storage layer and migration conventions. Enable and test the applicable integrity constraints rather than assuming the declaration alone enforces every invariant.

```sql
CREATE TABLE development_job (
    job_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    source_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    graph_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    model_set_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    profile_set_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    state TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (state IN (
        'queued', 'preparing', 'running', 'cancelling', 'cancelled',
        'verifying', 'ready_to_publish', 'published', 'failed'
    )),
    next_output_frame INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (next_output_frame >= 0),
    checkpoint_version INTEGER NOT NULL,
    output_contract_json TEXT NOT NULL,
    failure_code TEXT,
    created_at_utc TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at_utc TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE development_artifact (
    artifact_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    job_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES development_job(job_id),
    role TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (role IN (
        'source_reference', 'checkpoint', 'partial_output',
        'verified_output', 'published_output', 'evidence'
    )),
    location TEXT NOT NULL,
    content_hash TEXT,
    verified INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (verified IN (0, 1))
);
```

The state transition logic must enforce rules that SQL alone does not express. A job cannot become published before its output contract is verified. A cancelled job can retain a partial artifact without calling it complete. A failed evidence write must not remove a valid source reference. Test each transition with a transaction interruption and a process restart.

### B.22 Checkpoint identity and temporal reconstruction

A checkpoint is valid only for the exact source interpretation and processing graph that created it. Store the source identity, graph hash, profile set, model set, implementation version, output contract, completed interval, and temporal-state strategy. A hash of the recipe's display name is not sufficient.

```json
{
  "checkpoint_schema": 1,
  "job_id": "local-job-example",
  "source_hash": "sha256:replace-with-actual-source-digest",
  "graph_hash": "sha256:replace-with-actual-graph-digest",
  "model_set_hash": "sha256:replace-with-actual-model-set-digest",
  "profile_set_hash": "sha256:replace-with-actual-profile-set-digest",
  "next_output_frame": 240,
  "context_policy": {
    "kind": "recompute_overlap",
    "first_context_frame": 224,
    "discard_output_before": 240
  },
  "accepted_chunks": [],
  "status": "example_contract_not_a_real_checkpoint"
}
```

The example overlap is illustrative, not an algorithmic recommendation. Required context depends on the selected temporal model and state reconstruction method. Test the same job uninterrupted and interrupted at several boundaries. Compare output frame identities, timestamps, and image differences under the declared determinism policy. If exact equality is not guaranteed across backends, define the permitted numerical tolerance and preserve backend identity.

A model replacement, source edit, or profile update must invalidate incompatible state. The user may explicitly start a new job with the new components. Do not resume an old output with new weights merely because both models share a friendly name. This is a reproducibility failure even when the resulting clip is playable.

### B.23 Publication and cleanup as separate recoverable operations

The recorder and developer should stage output privately or through another explicitly owned temporary mechanism. Verification determines whether the artifact meets its output contract. Publication makes it visible in the intended library. Cleanup removes redundant temporary copies only after the durable published result is established. These are separate transitions.

Inject a failure after each transition. A failure before verification should leave a clearly labeled partial. A failure after verification but before publication should leave a verified local result that can be retried. A failure during provider copying should not delete the staging original. A failure after publication but before cleanup should leave duplicate storage that can be reconciled safely, not two unrelated clips with lost provenance.

Android's shared-media workflow includes platform-specific mechanisms relevant to pending items and access grants. Adapt the transaction to the actual supported API level and provider rather than assuming a local filesystem rename has equivalent semantics. The source and derived output may live in different storage systems.[^A07]

The recovery interface should explain the state using practical language. “Verified export awaiting publication” is different from “unfinished file; may not play.” A cleanup retry should not require rerendering a verified output. Deletion must target a specific artifact role, and the confirmation should identify whether the item is an original or a regenerable derivative.

### B.24 Untrusted imports and local privacy

Imported videos, profiles, recipes, and model packages are inputs, not trusted code. Validate their lengths, schemas, hashes, and allowed values before using them. Bound decompression, allocation, recursion, image dimensions, and string sizes. Reject path traversal and unexpected executable content in packages. A model package should not be allowed to run arbitrary installation scripts as part of ordinary import.

Use platform document access mechanisms with the narrowest practical grants. Do not request broad storage access solely to avoid implementing a proper picker. Keep access tokens, private file locations, and user identifiers out of public evidence bundles. A diagnostic export should make its contents inspectable before sharing.

Test denied permissions, revoked grants, moved files, unavailable providers, malformed JSON, oversized arrays, and packages with duplicate conflicting identifiers. A missing optional thumbnail should not make the source inaccessible. A missing required profile should block development with a specific explanation rather than silently choose a generic transform.

Offline operation should be testable by disabling network access after required local assets are installed. Capture, installed recipes, installed models, and development should continue according to their declared scope. Optional catalogue updates must not become hidden dependencies of opening a clip. No part of the core design requires sending video to a generative service.

### B.25 Movie catalogue schema: facts and reconstructions are different records

A catalogue should store claims separately from rendering recipes. This prevents an aesthetic parameter from being mistaken for a documented production fact. It also allows contradictory sources, scene-specific scopes, and revised scholarship without rewriting every recipe.

```sql
CREATE TABLE movie_record (
    movie_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    display_title TEXT NOT NULL,
    release_year INTEGER,
    alternate_titles_json TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE production_claim (
    claim_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    movie_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES movie_record(movie_id),
    proposition TEXT NOT NULL,
    scope TEXT NOT NULL,
    evidence_kind TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (evidence_kind IN (
        'documented', 'reconstructed', 'unknown', 'contradicted'
    )),
    source_references_json TEXT NOT NULL,
    review_state TEXT NOT NULL,
    reviewed_at_utc TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE look_recipe (
    recipe_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    movie_id TEXT REFERENCES movie_record(movie_id),
    scene_family TEXT NOT NULL,
    graph_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    required_source_contract_json TEXT NOT NULL,
    reconstruction_notes TEXT NOT NULL,
    version INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (version > 0)
);
```

The importer should reject a documented claim with no supporting reference, while allowing an explicitly unknown field. A reconstructed recipe can reference documented stock information without claiming that its numerical parameters came from the production. Search results should expose the distinction unobtrusively through labels and detail views.

Test alternate titles, duplicate imports, a revised source, conflicting claims, offline search, and a recipe whose required stock profile is not installed. The correct response to a missing dependency is a clear unavailable state or an explicit alternative recipe, not silent substitution under the original name.

### B.26 A worked movie-recipe research workflow

Choose one film and one scene family, not an entire cinematic universe. Collect primary production accounts and identify which statements are actually supported. Record whether the source discusses the whole production, a specific sequence, a camera unit, or an individual shot. Keep those scopes distinct.

For example, Kodak's account of *Oppenheimer* documents several stock choices and large-format workflows. That supports multiple research variants rather than one universal filter. The app's daylight color, low-light color, and monochrome reconstructions should preserve their separate evidence and assumptions.[^F05]

Next, define the reference version used for appearance evaluation. A theatrical print, digital cinema master, streamed copy, and HDR home release may not present identical appearance. Do not silently mix screenshots from different releases. Use appropriately authorized references and record display interpretation. When the reference's mastering details are unknown, mark the reconstruction exploratory.

Build a recipe from independently controlled components. First match broad tonal relationships using owned source footage with suitable lighting. Then assess color, texture scale, optical interpretation, and finishing. Avoid tuning all controls simultaneously because that makes causal diagnosis difficult. Save ablation renders and parameter history.

Finally, write a user-facing description explaining what the recipe is designed for and which parts are reconstructed. Do not claim that filming an unrelated scene with different lighting will reproduce the movie. The recipe is a controlled interpretation, not a substitute for cinematography.

### B.27 Camera interface acceptance

The main shooting interface should prioritize the preview, Record/Stop, recording state, selected source mode, elapsed time, audio status, and critical storage/thermal information. Secondary controls can live in bounded panels, but Record and Stop must remain reachable without scrolling. A panel should not destroy and recreate the preview surface merely because it opens.

Test portrait and landscape, larger text, screen-reader navigation, touch targets, and rapid panel changes. Distinguish drafts from applied settings. A user should be able to see whether a value is requested, effective, observed, unsupported, or pending. Do not display a misleading precise number when the camera reports unknown metadata.

The film and lens controls should be available without overwhelming acquisition decisions. A useful separation is Capture, Lens, Film, and Develop, with a clear indication of which controls affect the retained master and which affect only the derivative. Changing a preview recipe should not silently restart recording or alter the source format.

During a failure, preserve the most important action. A modal error should not hide Stop or prevent recovery. After a controlled stop, provide direct access to the retained result and its status. Test the interface with deliberately slow operations so progress and cancellation behavior are visible rather than assuming every device responds instantly.

### B.28 Monitoring aids must state their signal domain

A histogram, waveform, false-color overlay, or focus-peaking display is meaningful only in relation to the signal being measured. A display-preview histogram is not automatically a sensor exposure histogram. A Log waveform and an SDR waveform have different interpretations. The interface and evidence record should identify the monitored branch.

Construct a synthetic patch image with known values and verify the scope numerically before rendering it as a graphic. Test range endpoints, negative or out-of-range working values where applicable, and stale-frame behavior. A scope should indicate when it is unavailable or showing an older frame rather than presenting old data as live.

Preview scopes can operate at reduced resolution if that approximation is declared and acceptable for their purpose. They must not claim to certify sensor precision or optical focus. Sampling and downscaling can miss small clipped regions or fine detail. The diagnostic view should expose its limitations without making ordinary shooting cumbersome.

Test monitor independence by enabling every aid and confirming that the archival branch remains unchanged. Include orientation, crop, and letterboxing cases so guides align with the actual image. An overlay that looks centered on the screen may still be wrong relative to a cropped sensor region.

### B.29 A minimal evidence validator pattern

The following Python pattern illustrates fail-closed evidence validation. It is not part of the executed Appendix A suite and should receive its own tests before adoption. A production validator needs additional domain-specific requirements, artifact existence checks, cryptographic identity checks where appropriate, and schema migration support.

```python
from typing import Any

EXECUTION_STATES = {
    "passed", "failed", "blocked", "unavailable", "not_run", "inconclusive"
}

def validate_evidence(record: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    required = {"case_id", "claim", "outcome", "environment", "artifacts"}
    missing = required.difference(record)
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Missing evidence fields: {sorted(missing)}")
    if record["outcome"] not in EXECUTION_STATES:
        raise ValueError("Unknown execution outcome")
    if not isinstance(record["artifacts"], list):
        raise ValueError("Artifacts must be an explicit list")
    if record["outcome"] == "passed":
        if not record["artifacts"]:
            raise ValueError("A pass requires inspectable artifacts")
        if not record.get("oracle_result"):
            raise ValueError("A pass requires an oracle result")
    if record["outcome"] in {"blocked", "unavailable", "not_run", "inconclusive"}:
        if not record.get("reason"):
            raise ValueError("Non-passing evidence needs a reason")
    if record.get("physical_device_claim"):
        if record.get("environment", {}).get("kind") != "physical_device":
            raise ValueError("A nonphysical run cannot certify a physical-device claim")
```

Write tests for a valid host pass, a missing artifact, an unavailable hardware run, a synthetic run claiming physical certification, and an unknown outcome. Then test the report generator so it cannot discard failed rows or relabel unavailable as passed. The validator's existence is not enough; the release process must actually invoke it and preserve its failures.

### B.30 Continuous integration without false device certification

Use the repository's pinned toolchain and current test organization. The inspected README provides build and test commands, but this document did not execute the Android build. Revalidate those commands against the actual checked-out revision before relying on them.[^R01]

```sh
# Android repository commands from the inspected project documentation.
# Run against a verified checkout; retain complete output and exit status.
./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest :app:lintDebug :app:lintRelease \
  :app:assembleDebug :app:assembleRelease

# Requires an appropriate connected Android test environment.
./gradlew :app:connectedDebugAndroidTest

# Portable companion reference tests, from the reference directory.
python -m unittest -v test_reference.py
kotlinc kotlin/Contracts.kt kotlin/ContractsTest.kt -include-runtime -d contracts.jar
java -jar contracts.jar
```

Separate jobs by evidence class. Host numerical tests, Android unit tests, emulator instrumentation, codec probes, and physical-phone tests should have distinct names and artifacts. A hardware job that has no device must report unavailable or not run, not succeed by skipping its assertions. A build artifact can be published as a debug build without describing it as device-qualified.

Do not hide command failures with unconditional success operators. Preserve logs before cleanup. Pin dependencies and actions according to the repository's reviewed policy rather than copying unverified version numbers from a generic example. A change to the build environment should have its own baseline comparison so toolchain drift is not confused with an imaging regression.

### B.31 Release signing, updates, and retained media

Production signing belongs to the owner. Do not generate a disposable key and call the result a production release without an update policy. Do not place private keys, passwords, or account credentials in the repository, evidence bundle, or this directive. A debug artifact and a signed production artifact have different purposes and must be labeled accordingly.

Test application upgrades using the intended signing lineage and schema migrations. Existing clips, profiles, recipes, checkpoints, and evidence records should remain accessible or migrate explicitly. A failed migration must not delete originals. Keep a reversible backup strategy for metadata changes where practical, and test recovery from an interrupted migration.

Uninstall behavior matters because private application storage can contain retained originals and partial exports. The interface should make this clear and provide export paths. Do not recommend uninstalling as a routine fix without considering data retention. A troubleshooting flow should identify which data will be lost before suggesting destructive actions.

Release notes should state the supported evidence scope. For example, a version can add a host-verified renderer while physical 4K qualification remains pending. Avoid burying important limitations under a broad claim of cinematic quality. The update should make the product more useful without making its provenance harder to understand.

### B.32 End-to-end performance experiment

Define a workload before measuring it: source resolution, frame count, rate, color format, model, delegate, graph, quality settings, output codec, audio behavior, storage destination, and device state. Record whether the run is cold or warm. Keep the source identical between comparisons.

Measure wall-clock development time, per-stage latency, queue occupancy, memory high-water mark, output size, dropped or duplicated frames, cancellation latency, and thermal behavior. Use percentiles and maxima where relevant. Report initialization separately from steady state, but include both in the user-visible job duration.

Perform an ablation sequence. Start with decode and encode only, then add color conversion, depth, temporal refinement, optics, film response, grain, and final effects. This identifies the bottleneck and interactions. Do not infer total performance by adding isolated microbenchmarks if the integrated pipeline shares resources or overlaps work.

A useful optimization must preserve its quality contract. Compare images and timing before and after the change. If a faster mode uses reduced-resolution depth or fewer blur samples, save that distinction in the graph and expose it as a quality choice. An optimization that silently changes source precision or loses frames is a different product behavior, not merely a faster implementation.

### B.33 Film-rendering comparison protocol

Use identical clean input for the proposed renderer and any competing app or reference pipeline. Match output dimensions, cadence, range interpretation, and viewing conditions. Record which features and settings are enabled. A comparison of differently exposed camera recordings cannot isolate the quality of film emulation.

Construct a scene set covering neutral scales, skin, foliage, saturated objects, mixed lighting, specular highlights, deep shadows, smooth skies, fine texture, and motion. Include both favorable and difficult conditions. Avoid selecting only scenes that flatter the chosen stock interpretation.

For numerical review, inspect monotonicity, clipping, neutral behavior, grain scale, and temporal stability. For perceptual review, ask specific questions: which result has more plausible texture, less distracting halation, more stable motion boundaries, or a closer relationship to an authorized reference? Do not reduce every preference to one unexplained overall score.

Randomize presentation order and conceal labels when practical. Preserve individual responses and uncertainty. A small internal review can guide iteration but should not become a universal claim that the app is objectively superior. Publish the methodology alongside any broad quality claim, and retain the source clips so the comparison can be repeated after revisions.

### B.34 Canonical fixture library

The fixture library should be small enough to understand and broad enough to expose the main failure classes. Each fixture needs a stable identity, creation procedure, rights record, expected signal contract, and relevant phase mapping. The following list is a proposed starting set, not a claim that these media files are bundled.

| Fixture | Construction | Principal oracle |
|---|---|---|
| Signed exposure ramp | Synthetic values below black through high scene exposure | Encoding domain and monotonicity |
| Ten-bit code staircase | Known code levels entering the codec path | Independent decoded precision |
| Eight-bit-degraded staircase | Same source deliberately quantized earlier | False-positive precision rejection |
| Padded P010 rows | Known values with sentinel padding | Exact byte placement and bounds |
| Four CFA mosaics | Small known-color mosaics in each arrangement | Correct channel reconstruction |
| Truncated RAW sequence | Corruption at selected record boundaries | Rejection and prefix recovery policy |
| Moving timestamp marker | Each frame has a unique visible identity | Frame duplication and cadence |
| Flash-and-tone sequence | Repeatable audiovisual events | Offset and drift measurement |
| Neutral exposure wedge | Controlled capture over known exposure changes | Calibration and response consistency |
| Bright impulse field | Isolated sources at center and tile edges | Halation support and energy |
| Grain resolution pair | Same virtual geometry at two output sizes | Physical texture-scale consistency |
| Layered depth scene | Known foreground, focus plane, and background | Geometric defocus and ordering |
| Hair-like boundary scene | Fine moving strands against detail | Matting and temporal stability |
| Glass and reflection scene | Transparent and reflective surfaces | Confidence and conservative fallback |
| Crossing-subject scene | Two targets with explicit user selection | Focus identity and target loss |
| Hard-cut sequence | Unrelated scenes with continuous output timing | Temporal-state reset |
| Chunk-boundary motion | Motion and focus transition at resume boundary | Deterministic reconstruction |
| Storage-failure job | Injected failure during publish and cleanup | Source retention and retry state |
| Catalogue contradiction | Conflicting scoped production claims | Evidence preservation |
| Accessibility stress layout | Large text and alternate input modes | Reachable controls and readable states |

The library should contain synthetic fixtures for exact oracles and owned real footage for difficult appearance. Do not replace one category with the other. Record which fixture is appropriate for each claim, and add a new fixture whenever a real defect escapes the existing set.

### B.35 The firmware investigation notebook

Firmware research begins with a specific question: which useful stream or control appears blocked, what public evidence supports its existence, and at which layer does the failure occur? Record the exact device variant and current software. Separate observations from hypotheses. A failed app configuration is not proof of a HAL restriction, and a HAL restriction is not proof that the sensor supports the desired sustained mode.

Start with non-destructive inspection, public metadata, controlled session attempts, logs available through authorized development access, and comparison of supported routes. Preserve reproducible inputs and failure codes. Do not write a generic flashing procedure into the ordinary app workflow.

Before any action that modifies device software, require explicit authorization for that action, a risk review, backup considerations, and a credible recovery plan. Relevant hardware-backed security state may be irreversible. The user's general interest in firmware does not authorize every risky operation automatically.[^S03]

A useful outcome can be a well-supported decision not to proceed. If the blocked capability would not materially improve the film and optics product, prioritize the application-level path. If a safe experiment reveals a viable new route, keep it experimental until its image quality, timing, storage, thermal behavior, and recovery have been measured independently.

### B.36 Failure taxonomy and triage

Classify failures by what was violated: source integrity, interpretation, numerical precision, timing, ownership, storage, temporal geometry, appearance, interaction, provenance, rights, or environment availability. This helps prevent every visual problem from being labeled a model problem or every camera error from being blamed on firmware.

A triage record should include the smallest reproducing source, graph, device or host environment, observed behavior, expected contract, first affected frame or operation, relevant logs, and whether the source remains intact. Preserve the original failing artifact before attempting repairs. A repair that overwrites the only reproducer makes future verification difficult.

Use component ablations to isolate the defect. Replace estimated depth with perfect synthetic depth, disable temporal reuse, bypass film response, use the CPU reference, or remove optional preview work. Each ablation answers a specific hypothesis. Do not change many settings at once and then claim to know the cause because the symptom disappeared.

Prioritize footage loss, silent lineage mislabeling, false certification, and reproducible crashes before aesthetic refinements. A severe failure should block the affected route even when most clips look good. Keep the rest of the application usable where its independent contracts remain satisfied.

### B.37 Evidence handoff example

A handoff is a compact scientific report, not a celebratory summary. It must allow another developer to reproduce the result and identify what remains uncertain. Use stable phase and case identifiers from this directive, and link local artifacts by actual paths or repository references that exist.

```json
{
  "phase_id": "P105",
  "status": "software_verified_physical_pending",
  "source_revision": "replace-with-actual-commit",
  "implemented_contracts": ["replace-with-observed-behavior"],
  "executed_tests": [],
  "negative_controls": [],
  "artifacts": [],
  "physical_device_evidence": null,
  "remaining_gates": ["replace-with-specific-unexecuted-protocol"],
  "next_dependency_ready_phase": null,
  "example_only": true
}
```

The placeholders make this an explicit template, not a claimed result. Production reports must replace them with actual values and must not leave empty test lists while claiming broad verification. When only a subset of a phase is complete, identify the subset by contract rather than guessing a percentage.

The next step should follow evidence. If a codec route is unavailable, investigate another qualified interface or keep the feature unavailable. If a depth renderer fails at hair boundaries, improve the boundary model or restrict aggressive settings. Do not respond to every incomplete gate by adding more stock names or interface decoration.

### B.38 Quality tiers and experimental labeling

A release can expose different evidence tiers without confusing the user. A stable tier contains routes and effects with the required software and device evidence for their advertised scope. An experimental tier contains useful research paths with explicit limitations. A diagnostic tier exposes candidates and measurements without offering them as ordinary recording choices.

The tier belongs to a specific configuration, not to the entire application forever. A particular lens, resolution, codec, and graph may be stable while another remains experimental. A stock interpretation may be visually reviewed but not colorimetrically calibrated. A depth effect may be acceptable at restrained settings but unreliable at extreme blur.

Tests must verify that the interface preserves these distinctions. A recipe cannot promote an experimental capture mode into a stable one. A successful short test cannot erase a pending endurance gate. A ten-bit export cannot promote an SDR source into RAW-derived status. Historical evidence remains tied to the revision and configuration that produced it.

Experimental labeling is not permission for careless data loss. Original retention, cancellation, privacy, and truthful reporting remain mandatory. The difference is the supported claim and default availability, not whether the implementation is allowed to ignore basic safety and integrity contracts.

### B.39 A research plan for metric depth

Metric depth is an optional advanced path, not a prerequisite for useful relative-depth rendering. Begin by defining the intended distance range, camera route, capture geometry, and acceptable uncertainty. Decide whether calibration uses known objects, controlled targets, multiple views, device metadata, or a separately justified estimator. Record the assumptions before collecting data.

Use a training or fitting set and an independent validation set spanning the intended range. Measure reference distances with a documented method and uncertainty. Avoid evaluating only one planar target under one lighting condition. Test textured and weakly textured surfaces, foreground/background combinations, and camera motion where relevant.

Report scale and offset errors, local ordering, boundary behavior, and temporal drift separately. A low average distance error can coexist with unusable focus jumps. The UI should display metric values only when the active model and calibration satisfy the selected qualification policy. Otherwise it should return to relative controls without fabricating precision.

Compare the resulting optical behavior against the perfect-depth renderer. This separates distance-estimation error from point-spread rendering error. Keep the source's original optical blur in the analysis: matching a target focus plane cannot restore detail already blurred by the phone lens or motion exposure.

### B.40 Final implementation decision checklist

Before declaring the integrated app ready for a user trial, inspect one complete journey from capture or import to retained source, recipe selection, local development, verification, publication, revision, and export. Every transition must preserve identity and explain its state. A polished preview alone does not demonstrate the journey.

Confirm that all six requested formats exist as coherent geometry and texture interpretations, not merely names. Confirm that stock, optics, development, and finishing remain independently represented. Confirm that the movie catalogue separates sourced claims from reconstruction. Confirm that installed models and recipes work offline and that original footage is not sent to an undisclosed service.

Review difficult complete clips rather than selected stills. Inspect hair, glass, foreground blur, scene cuts, focus transitions, smooth gradients, highlights, and shadows. Review recovery after cancellation, storage pressure, and process interruption. Keep any unresolved severe failures visible in the release decision.

Finally, read the user-facing claims alongside the actual evidence. Replace unsupported language with precise descriptions. The product should promise controllable film-inspired rendering, optional computational optics, and the best verified capture route available on the tested phone configuration. It should not promise that software has physically transformed the S23 Ultra into an ARRI or IMAX camera.


### B.41 Manual corrections and nondestructive local overrides

A useful computational lens should allow correction rather than insist that the model is always right. Design a local override system for focus targets, foreground/background ordering, conservative exclusion regions, and selected keyframes. The first version can be restrained: a user marks a region that should remain protected from aggressive defocus, or corrects the relative ordering of two surfaces. Do not begin with a complex editor that prevents the core renderer from shipping.

Overrides are graph inputs, not edits to the original footage. Store their coordinate system, source frame reference, temporal extent, interpolation rule, and authoring version. A screen-space brush stroke must be transformed correctly when the preview is letterboxed, cropped, stabilized, or rotated. Test a known point through the complete coordinate chain in both directions. An apparently small coordinate error can put a correction on the wrong side of a face or fence.

Temporal propagation must be explicit. A correction can apply to one frame, a bounded interval, a tracked region, or a whole shot. Each mode has different assumptions. If tracking loses the region, the application should stop propagation or reduce confidence according to policy rather than apply the correction to an unrelated object. Preserve keyframes so the user can inspect and revise the propagation.

Test overrides against perfect synthetic depth before combining them with estimated depth. Then test a difficult real sequence where the automatic model fails. Verify that the correction improves the intended region without creating new temporal discontinuities at its start and end. A smooth transition is not always correct; a hard scene cut should still reset the relevant state.

Exported recipes should distinguish reusable artistic settings from source-specific corrections. A brush mask tied to one clip should not accidentally become part of a movie preset applied to every future recording. The job manifest must retain the correction identity so the developed output remains reproducible.

### B.42 A quantitative acceptance registry

Create one registry for acceptance policies rather than scattering unexplained thresholds through tests and shaders. Each entry needs a metric name, units, domain, fixture class, sampling rule, threshold, uncertainty treatment, version, rationale, and owner. Mark values as inherited project policy, provisional research policy, or externally specified requirements where a genuine specification applies.

```json
{
  "metric_id": "example.temporal_boundary_review",
  "policy_version": 1,
  "status": "provisional_project_policy",
  "measurement_domain": "complete developed clip at declared display transform",
  "units": "review categories and per-frame diagnostic measurements",
  "sampling": "all frames plus normal-speed full-clip viewing",
  "threshold": null,
  "threshold_state": "must_be_defined_before_experiment",
  "rationale": "prevent a favorable average from hiding severe intermittent artifacts",
  "scope": "selected graph, source class, quality mode, and tested device configuration"
}
```

The null threshold is intentional in this example. It is not permission to pass the experiment without a policy. The phase owner must choose and justify an appropriate criterion before the qualifying run. Some appearance judgments require a rubric rather than a single scalar threshold; the registry should support that honestly.

When a threshold changes, retain the old policy and results. Re-evaluate whether the new policy requires rerunning earlier evidence. Do not relabel an old failed output as passed without explaining the policy revision. Conversely, a stricter new policy should not pretend that an earlier release was tested under conditions that did not exist at the time.

The report generator should include metric units and policy versions automatically. A number without its domain is ambiguous: an error measured in linear RGB, Log code values, decoded YUV, or display pixels answers different questions. Test serialization and aggregation so units, exclusions, and uncertainty do not disappear when results move from detailed logs into a summary dashboard.

### B.43 HDR monitoring and ordinary-display compatibility

The application may capture or develop material whose signal cannot be shown directly on every display. Monitoring is therefore an interpretation step. Maintain a clear distinction between the encoded master, an HDR viewing path where supported, and an SDR monitoring transform. A display-compatible preview is not permission to rewrite the master with that transform.

Test the same source through both monitoring branches using known patches and independently inspected output descriptors. Verify that switching the monitor does not alter the saved source, graph, or clean master. Where the device cannot support the selected combination of capture and preview streams, explain the limitation rather than silently substituting a different acquisition format.

A generic gallery application may interpret Log footage incorrectly or ignore a sidecar. That does not necessarily mean the encoded values are wrong, but it does mean the user needs a clear workflow. Provide a properly rendered viewing derivative or an in-app color-managed preview, and document the correct editor assignment for the master. Interoperability tests should name the consumer version and settings rather than claim universal automatic detection.

Do not use a visually pleasing preview as the only validation of color signaling. Inspect decoded values and metadata independently. Conversely, correct tags do not guarantee that a particular display path renders them correctly. Both numerical and viewing checks are necessary, and their evidence should remain separate.

### B.44 Research exceptions and bounded experiments

A research directive must allow experimentation without allowing every experiment to redefine the product silently. Create an exception record when a prototype deliberately violates a normal production constraint, such as using a slow CPU reference, an uncalibrated synthetic stock, a temporary full-frame allocation, or an offline workstation model for comparison. State the purpose, affected scope, duration of the exception in project terms, and conditions for removal.

An exception must never waive original retention, honest labeling, or required authorization for risky device actions. It may permit a deliberately slow reference renderer because correctness is being established before optimization. It may not permit deleting source footage to conceal a storage defect. It may permit a synthetic profile for a synthetic fixture. It may not permit that profile to certify physical S23 footage.

Keep experimental outputs out of the ordinary accepted-media path unless they are clearly labeled and the user explicitly requests them. A researcher may need to inspect a failed render or a partial file; that is different from publishing it as a verified result. The application should support investigation without confusing diagnostic artifacts with finished clips.

Close each experiment with a decision: adopt the method, revise the hypothesis, retain it as a reference, defer it pending evidence, or reject it for the intended scope. Record why. A negative result can save substantial development effort when it identifies an unsupported assumption. The directive's purpose is not to force every proposed technique into the final app, but to produce the strongest coherent application supported by the evidence.


### B.45 The first complete user trial

The first trial should demonstrate a small, complete workflow rather than every experimental feature. Use one verified source route or a clearly identified imported clip, one restrained virtual lens, and a small set of film interpretations. Retain the original, develop locally, inspect the result, revise one parameter, and export both a viewing copy and the appropriate master or provenance record.

During that trial, observe whether the user understands which controls affect capture and which affect development. Record any confusion about format names, focus distance, calibration status, export interpretation, or source deletion. These observations become testable interface requirements, not reasons to hide the underlying distinctions.

The trial succeeds only within its declared scope. It establishes that the integrated journey is usable and that its outputs can be traced and recovered. It does not certify every lens, stock, resolution, frame rate, firmware variant, or difficult scene. Expand the scope through subsequent recorded qualification, preserving the same standards of evidence.


<a id="artifact-verification"></a>
## Appendix C. Artifact verification and evidence boundary

This artifact was assembled from an authored research core, 160 individually specified phase records, 160 workstream-specific adversarial condition records, and their 1,280 explicit phase-condition combinations. Each combination retains the phase fixture and baseline oracle so it can be reviewed independently. A machine-readable companion manifest carries the same identifiers and dependencies.

The document verifier checks phase count, case count, identifier uniqueness, dependency validity, source-footnote resolution, internal anchor resolution, balanced code fences, minimum requested length, and absence of unresolved assembly markers. These checks assess the artifact’s structure, not the correctness of every future implementation decision.

Actual host execution during artifact preparation:

| Evidence | Result | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Python initial red run | 48 tests failed at unimplemented boundaries | Test-first host reference |
| Python boundary-hardening red run | 5 new tests failed; 48 existing tests passed | Overflow and evidence-type contracts |
| Python final green run | 53 tests passed | Included Python fixtures only |
| Kotlin complete red run | 0 passed; 32 failed | Test-first portable contracts |
| Kotlin final green run | 32 passed; 0 failed | Included JVM checks only |
| Android application build | Not performed for this document | No APK certification |
| Physical S23 Ultra testing | Not performed | No sensor, lens, thermal, or throughput certification |
| Expanded laboratory catalogue | Specifications only | Not 1,280 executed tests |

The complete run logs are supplied in the companion bundle. Do not convert this table into a production-release claim. Subsequent development must create new evidence tied to the actual Android revision and physical configuration.
